questions.answer: An Argo CD Application points to a Git repository and chart path or a Helm repository plus version, target cluster and namespace, and approved values. Argo renders Helm templates itself, compares them with live state and applies changes according to sync policy. Automated sync, prune and self-heal are separate choices. Health checks, sync waves, projects and RBAC constrain ordering and tenancy.

questions.question: Do you have experience with Helm charts, including deploying common components across clusters and managing similar deployments for multiple microservices?
questions.answer: Yes. I use Helm to package reusable Kubernetes resources such as Deployments, Services, service accounts, autoscaling, disruption budgets, ConfigMaps, Ingress or Gateway resources and policy-compatible security settings. A common library chart holds approved labels, probes, resource configuration and security defaults, while each microservice supplies a small values file for image digest, ports, capacity and environment-specific integration. For shared components such as monitoring agents, policy controllers or security defenders, I maintain a separately versioned chart and deploy it through GitOps to selected clusters using cluster-specific values and staged rollout rings. CI runs `helm lint`, renders templates, validates schemas and Kubernetes policy, scans images and tests upgrades before publishing an immutable chart version. I avoid one chart with excessive conditionals, never place secret values in ordinary values files and document ownership, supported versions, rollback and CRD handling.

questions.question: Why avoid deploying every production microservice simultaneously, and how do you coordinate dependent releases?
questions.answer: Release independently deployable services separately to limit blast radius and make a regression attributable to a specific version. Use backward-compatible APIs, consumer contract tests, expand-and-contract database changes and feature flags so old and new versions can coexist. Coordinate truly dependent services with a tested version compatibility matrix and staged rollout order; a shared Git commit or Argo CD sync is not an atomic transaction across services. Use canaries and stop conditions based on business errors, latency and saturation. For an unavoidable release train, prepare per-service rollback and verify data compatibility before reverting.

questions.question: What Kubernetes production rollout settings and initial CPU/memory requests and limits would you choose across environments?
questions.answer: Review immutable image digest, configuration/secrets, readiness/startup/liveness probes, replicas, rollout maxSurge/maxUnavailable, graceful termination, security context, placement, disruption budgets, autoscaling and downstream capacity. There is no universal safe resource size. For a small stateless service, 100m CPU and 128Mi memory requests with a 256Mi memory limit can be a load-test starting point, not a production recommendation; Java or memory-heavy services may require much more. Set memory requests from observed working set with headroom and limits above safe peak usage; memory-limit breaches can cause OOM kills. CPU limits throttle rather than kill, and some latency-sensitive platforms omit them under controlled policy. CPU HPA utilization uses requests as its denominator. Dev/QA can use fewer replicas and less capacity, while UAT/load testing should preserve production behavior and realistic per-instance sizing. Validate startup, peak traffic, failure recovery and rollout surge before approval.

questions.question: Explain Requests and Limits.
questions.answer: A resource request is the CPU or memory amount Kubernetes uses for scheduling and, for CPU, relative runtime weighting. A limit is the maximum a container may consume. Exceeding a CPU limit causes throttling; exceeding a memory limit can trigger an OOM kill. If requests are too low, nodes become overcommitted and unstable; if too high, Pods remain Pending and capacity is wasted. Set values from observed usage and load tests, monitor throttling and OOM events, and use LimitRange or policy controls to prevent unbounded workloads.

questions.question: CI/CD design: Design a safe promotion workflow from commit to production using GitHub Actions, Cloud Build, Jenkins, artifact promotion, approvals, and rollback.
questions.answer: Trigger CI on commit to build, test, and produce one immutable artifact tagged with the git SHA, scan it for vulnerabilities, and promote that exact artifact through dev -> staging -> production by updating deployment references rather than rebuilding. Gate production promotion behind a required approval (a human reviewer or automated staging metric check), and keep the previous production artifact reference readily available so rollback is a fast, low-risk redeploy rather than a new build under pressure.

questions.question: Who writes and owns the tests run in the deployment pipeline?
questions.answer: Application developers usually own unit and component tests, QA/SDET teams may own broader integration and end-to-end suites, and security specialists define required security checks. Platform/DevOps engineers provide reliable execution environments, test-data/secrets integration, pipeline gates and result reporting, and often write infrastructure or deployment smoke tests. The actual split is team-specific. State the tests and pipeline code you personally wrote, distinguish integrating a suite from authoring it, and describe how failures block promotion and reach the responsible owner.

questions.question: How do you manage production release approvals and ServiceNow/CAB changes?
questions.answer: Link the immutable release artifact to tested results, security disposition, QA/UAT sign-off where required, implementation plan, customer impact, change window, owner, validation criteria and rollback plan in the change record. A designated change authority approves according to risk; a CAB is a policy-specific review mechanism, not a mandatory meeting for every low-risk deployment. Standard changes may be pre-authorized, while emergency changes follow a recorded emergency approval path. The pipeline checks the authorized environment, requester, approved change and deployment identity before promotion and writes execution status back to ServiceNow. Keep segregation of duties and an audit trail. Familiarity with ServiceNow should be described through work actually performed, such as raising changes, attaching evidence or integrating APIs, rather than claiming administrator experience.

questions.question: Explain Infrastructure as Code.
questions.answer:
Infrastructure as Code means managing infrastructure using version-controlled code rather than manual console changes. It improves repeatability, reviewability, automation, compliance, and disaster recovery.

Detailed interview explanation:
Infrastructure As Code should be explained as part of Infrastructure as Code. Terraform lets teams define infrastructure declaratively, review changes before applying them, and keep cloud resources aligned with version-controlled configuration. The important production concerns are state management, dependency ordering, module reuse, drift detection, policy enforcement, and secure automation.

Production example:
In an enterprise Terraform workflow, an engineer raises a pull request for infrastructure changes. CI runs terraform fmt, validate, security scanning, cost checks, and terraform plan. Reviewers inspect the plan before apply. Production applies are executed by a controlled pipeline identity, while state is stored in a remote encrypted backend with locking and restricted access.

Best practices to mention:
- Use remote encrypted state with locking and backups.
- Split large infrastructure into modules and separate state boundaries.
- Pin provider and module versions.
- Avoid storing secrets in code, outputs, or broadly accessible state.
- Use policy-as-code and drift detection before production changes.

Common interview follow-ups:
Be ready to explain state corruption, partial applies, imports, state migration, workspaces, module design, provider authentication, and how to recover when Terraform state and real infrastructure do not match.

questions.question: How did you use Terraform in your recent GCP project, and can you give a specific automation example?
questions.answer:
In my recent project, I used Terraform extensively to automate and standardize GCP infrastructure provisioning. We maintained a centralized repository of versioned, reusable modules for VPC networking, service accounts and IAM, GKE, load balancers, Cloud Armor, Cloud Run, storage buckets and Secret Manager. Application or live-environment repositories consumed pinned module versions and supplied environment-specific values through reviewed variable files rather than duplicating resource definitions.

Terraform ran through Bitbucket Pipelines. A pull request triggered formatting, validation, security or policy checks and a `terraform plan`; reviewers examined the exact proposed change. After approval, the controlled deployment stage applied the reviewed configuration using a dedicated least-privilege service account, so normal infrastructure changes did not require engineers to create resources manually in the GCP console. Dev, QA, UAT and Production had separate state boundaries to reduce blast radius. Remote state was stored in a restricted, versioned GCS bucket using the backend's locking behavior, with audit logging and recovery controls. IAM bindings and Organization Policies were also managed as code to keep environments consistent.

A strong example was external-application onboarding. Instead of manually configuring every network and security component, reusable modules created the external load balancer, backend service or NEG configuration, approved custom headers, TLS and domain integration, Cloud Armor policy and rate limits, service accounts, IAM and supporting monitoring resources. The application team supplied a small contract containing the project, environment, backend, domain, capacity and security parameters. The pipeline validated those inputs and produced an auditable plan. This reduced onboarding lead time, eliminated repeated console work and made the resulting infrastructure repeatable, reviewable and easier to detect for drift. I would quantify the actual time or error reduction where project measurements are available.

questions.question: How do applications or pods running on GKE securely access GCP services such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Secret Manager and Cloud SQL?
questions.answer: I use Workload Identity Federation for GKE so each Kubernetes service account receives only the IAM permissions required by its workload, without a downloaded key. Depending on the supported pattern, I grant the Kubernetes principal direct resource permissions or bind it to a Google service account; the Pod uses Application Default Credentials and the metadata service obtains short-lived tokens. Cloud Storage and BigQuery permissions are scoped to the required bucket, dataset or table; Secret Manager access is scoped to named secrets; and Cloud SQL uses private IP or an approved connector plus database authentication and authorization. Network paths use private Google access, Private Service Connect or private service access where appropriate, and egress policy permits only required destinations. I keep Kubernetes RBAC separate from Google Cloud IAM, audit both, test denied access and avoid granting broad project roles to the cluster node service account.

questions.question: What is a DaemonSet?
questions.answer: A DaemonSet ensures exactly one copy of a Pod runs on every node (or a selected subset via node selectors/affinity) in the cluster, automatically adding a Pod to any new node that joins and removing it when a node leaves - used for node-level agents like log collectors, monitoring exporters, or CNI/storage plugins that need to run everywhere.

questions.question: What is a StatefulSet?
questions.answer:
A StatefulSet in Kubernetes is a Kubernetes workload resource used to manage stateful applications that require:
      * Stable pod identities
      * Persistent storage
      * Ordered deployment and scaling
Unlike Deployments, StatefulSets give each Pod:
      * A unique name
      * Stable network identity
      * Dedicated persistent volume
Common Use Cases
      * Databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB)
      * Kafka
      * Elasticsearch
      * Redis clusters
Key Features
Predictable Pod names
Example:
mysql-0
mysql-1
mysql-2
      *       * Persistent storage for each Pod
      * Pods restart with same identity and storage
      * Ordered startup and shutdown
Difference from Deployment
Deployment
	StatefulSet
	Used for stateless apps
	Used for stateful apps
	Pod names change
	Stable Pod names
	Shared/temporary storage
	Persistent dedicated storage
	Pods created randomly
	Pods created sequentially
	Important Interview Point
If a database Pod restarts, it must reconnect with the same storage and identity. StatefulSet guarantees this behavior.
One-Line Summary
StatefulSet is used to manage stateful applications in Kubernetes with stable identities and persistent storage.

questions.question: What is the Kubernetes Cloud Controller Manager?
questions.answer: The cloud-controller-manager runs cloud-specific control loops that integrate Kubernetes with a cloud provider, separating them from the core kube-controller-manager. Depending on the implementation, it initializes cloud-derived node information, handles removed cloud instances, manages routes and reconciles cloud load balancers for Services. Its exact responsibilities differ by provider and managed service; not every Ingress/Gateway controller is part of the cloud controller manager. The API server stores desired objects and controllers call provider APIs to reconcile infrastructure. It is control-plane automation rather than a proxy traversed by every application request.

questions.question: Explain Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA).
questions.answer: HPA automatically adjusts the number of Pod replicas for a Deployment/StatefulSet based on observed metrics (CPU/memory via metrics-server by default, or custom/external metrics like request rate via Prometheus Adapter), scaling out under load and back in when load drops, within a configured min/max replica range. It requires resource requests to be set on the Pods, since scaling decisions are based on utilization relative to requests.

questions.question: Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets: What are ConfigMaps and Secrets, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration data (environment variables, config files) that pods can consume as env vars or mounted files; Secrets are structurally similar but intended for sensitive data (though only base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default) like credentials or tokens. Use ConfigMaps for anything safe to view in plaintext, and Secrets (ideally backed by an external secret manager via CSI driver) for anything sensitive.

questions.question: When a ConfigMap changes, how do running pods receive the new configuration?
questions.answer: Environment-variable values from a ConfigMap are fixed when the container starts and require a new Pod. Mounted ConfigMap volumes are updated eventually by the kubelet, but applications must watch and safely reload the file; `subPath` mounts do not receive normal updates. I choose explicit reload or controlled rollout based on application behavior and never assume a ConfigMap change automatically restarts Pods.

questions.question: Explain Node Affinity.
questions.answer:
Node affinity is a scheduling feature in Kubernetes that lets you control which nodes a Pod can or should run on based on node labels.
________________


Core idea
Node affinity tells the scheduler: “Place this Pod on nodes that match these rules.”
It is a more expressive and flexible replacement for nodeSelector.
________________


Why node affinity is used
It helps you:
      * Run workloads on specific hardware (GPU, SSD, high-memory nodes)
      * Separate environments (dev, staging, prod)
      * Control placement across zones/regions
      * Optimize performance and cost
________________


How it works
Nodes have labels like:
disktype: ssd
zone: us-east-1a
gpu: true
Pod defines affinity rules to match these labels.
________________


Types of node affinity
1. Required (Hard rule)
Pod MUST run only on matching nodes
      * Strict constraint
      * If no node matches → Pod stays Pending
Example:
nodeAffinity:
  requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - key: disktype
        operator: In
        values:
        - ssd
________________


2. Preferred (Soft rule)
Scheduler tries best to match, but not mandatory
      * Used for optimization, not restriction
      * Pod still runs if no preferred node exists
Example:
nodeAffinity:
  preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
  - weight: 1
    preference:
      matchExpressions:
      - key: zone
        operator: In
        values:
        - us-east-1a
________________


Operators used
      * In
      * NotIn
      * Exists
      * DoesNotExist
      * Gt, Lt
________________


Node affinity vs nodeSelector
Feature
	nodeSelector
	node affinity
	Flexibility
	Low
	High
	Logic
	Exact match
	Complex expressions
	Required/Preferred
	No
	Yes
	Use case
	Simple scheduling
	Advanced scheduling
	________________


Types of affinity scope
1. During scheduling
      * Controls initial placement
2. During execution
      * IgnoredDuringExecution means:
      * If node labels change after scheduling, Pod is NOT evicted
________________


Simple analogy
Think of it like job placement:
      * Node labels = company locations & facilities
      * Pod = employee
      * Node affinity = “I want to work in a city with a data center and SSD storage”
________________


Interview-ready definition
Node affinity in Kubernetes is a scheduling mechanism that allows pods to be assigned to nodes based on node labels using flexible rules, supporting both required (hard constraints) and preferred (soft preferences) conditions for pod placement.

questions.question: Explain Pod Affinity.
questions.answer: Pod affinity influences scheduling by requiring or preferring a Pod to run near other Pods matching specified labels. Rules use a label selector and a `topologyKey`, such as `kubernetes.io/hostname` for the same node or a zone label for the same availability zone. `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` is mandatory; if no node satisfies it, the Pod remains Pending. `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` adds weighted preferences without blocking scheduling. Affinity can reduce latency, but excessive co-location harms failure isolation and can make scheduling slow or impossible.

questions.question: What is Pod Anti-Affinity and how does it differ from Pod Affinity?
questions.answer: Pod affinity attracts a Pod toward nodes or topology domains containing Pods that match a label selector; anti-affinity separates them. For example, required anti-affinity on kubernetes.io/hostname prevents matching replicas sharing a node, while a preferred rule makes separation a best-effort scheduling preference. topologyKey defines the domain, such as node or zone, and namespace scoping determines which existing Pods are matched. Required rules can leave Pods Pending when there are too few eligible domains. These rules influence placement, not packet filtering; topology spread constraints are often useful when the requirement is balanced distribution rather than strict pairwise separation.

questions.question: Explain Taints and Tolerations.
questions.answer:
Taints and tolerations in Kubernetes are mechanisms used to control which Pods are allowed to run on which Nodes.
They work together to implement node-level restrictions and exceptions.
________________


Core idea
Taints are applied on nodes (to repel pods)
Tolerations are applied on pods (to allow them in)
So:
      * Taint = “Stay away from me” (node says this)
      * Toleration = “I can tolerate this condition” (pod says this)
________________


1. Taints
A taint is applied to a node to prevent unwanted pods from scheduling there.
Format:
key=value:effect
________________


Effects of taints
1. NoSchedule
      * Pods without toleration will NOT be scheduled
2. PreferNoSchedule
      * Kubernetes tries to avoid placing pods, but not strict
3. NoExecute
      * Existing pods are also evicted immediately
________________


Example taint
kubectl taint nodes node1 key=dedicated:NoSchedule
This means:
“Do not schedule normal pods on this node”
________________


2. Tolerations
A toleration is defined in a Pod to allow it to be scheduled onto a tainted node.
It does NOT force scheduling—only allows it.
________________


Example toleration
tolerations:
- key: "dedicated"
  operator: "Equal"
  value: "dev"
  effect: "NoSchedule"
________________


Meaning
“This pod is allowed to run on nodes tainted with dedicated=dev:NoSchedule”
________________


How they work together
Node (Taint)
	Pod (Toleration)
	Result
	No taint
	Any pod
	Allowed
	Taint exists
	No toleration
	Blocked
	Taint exists
	Matching toleration
	Allowed
	________________


Real-world use cases
1. Dedicated nodes
      * GPU nodes only for ML workloads
2. System nodes
      * Only system pods allowed
3. Isolation
      * Separate dev / prod workloads
4. Critical workloads
      * Ensure important services get reserved nodes
________________


Example scenario
Node:
kubectl taint nodes gpu-node gpu=true:NoSchedule
Pod:
tolerations:
- key: "gpu"
  operator: "Equal"
  value: "true"
  effect: "NoSchedule"
Only GPU-enabled pods can run there.
________________


Important concept
      * Taints repel pods
      * Tolerations do not attract pods
To attract pods, you need:
      * Node affinity or nodeSelector
________________


Taints vs Node Affinity
Feature
	Taints & Tolerations
	Node Affinity
	Purpose
	Block unwanted pods
	Prefer/require nodes
	Direction
	Node → Pod (repel)
	Pod → Node (select)
	Use case
	Isolation
	Placement control
	________________


Simple analogy
Think of a club:
      * Taint = “VIP-only entry”
      * Toleration = “I have VIP pass”
      * Node affinity = “I want to go to this club”
________________


Interview-ready definition
Taints and tolerations in Kubernetes are mechanisms used to control pod scheduling by allowing nodes to repel certain pods using taints, while pods can explicitly declare tolerations to override these restrictions and be scheduled onto those nodes.

questions.question: What is a service mesh?
questions.answer: A service mesh is an infrastructure layer (like Istio) that manages service-to-service communication - routing, retries, mTLS encryption, observability - via sidecar proxies, without requiring changes to application code.

questions.question: What is Istio?
questions.answer: Istio is a Kubernetes-native service mesh that transparently injects Envoy sidecar proxies to handle traffic management, security, and observability for microservices. Its control plane (istiod) configures data‑plane proxies and exposes APIs like VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway for traffic routing, PeerAuthentication/AuthorizationPolicy for mTLS and RBAC, and Telemetry integration with Prometheus/Jaeger. Operators install with istioctl install and verify control plane pods via kubectl get pods -n istio-system and sidecar injection by checking pod containers (kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'). Use istioctl proxy-status and istioctl analyze for runtime and config validation.

questions.question: Kubernetes Service types: What is a Service, and how do ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer differ?
questions.answer: A Service provides a stable network endpoint and DNS name that load-balances traffic across a set of pods matching a label selector, decoupling clients from individual pod IPs that change as pods are rescheduled. ClusterIP (the default) is only reachable inside the cluster; NodePort additionally exposes the service on a static port on every node's IP; LoadBalancer provisions an external cloud load balancer (e.g. a GCP Network/HTTPS LB) that routes external traffic to the service.

questions.question: Kubernetes architecture: Explain the architecture of Kubernetes, including control plane and worker-node components.
questions.answer: The control plane consists of the API server (the front door for all cluster interactions), etcd (stores cluster state), the scheduler (assigns pods to nodes), and controller managers (reconcile actual state toward desired state). Worker nodes run the kubelet (talks to the API server and manages containers on that node), a container runtime, and kube-proxy (handles Service networking) - together the control plane decides what should run and workers actually run it.

questions.question: Explain continuous deployment.
questions.answer:
What is Continuous Deployment?
Continuous Deployment is a software delivery practice where every code change that passes all automated tests and quality checks is automatically deployed to production without any manual intervention.
It is the final stage of CI/CD automation.
________________


How It Works
Developer Commit
       ↓
Build Application
       ↓
Run Automated Tests
       ↓
Code Quality Checks
       ↓
Security Scans
       ↓
Create Artifact/Docker Image
       ↓
Deploy to Production Automatically
If all stages succeed, the application is released to users immediately.
________________


Example
Suppose a developer fixes a bug and pushes code to GitHub:
               1. CI pipeline is triggered.
               2. Application is built.
               3. Unit and integration tests run.
               4. Security and quality scans pass.
               5. Docker image is created and pushed to a registry.
               6. Kubernetes deployment is updated automatically.
               7. Users receive the new version without any manual approval.
________________


Benefits
               * Faster release cycles
               * Reduced manual effort
               * Immediate delivery of features and fixes
               * Lower deployment risk through small, frequent changes
               * Consistent and repeatable deployments
________________


Challenges
               * Requires strong automated testing
               * Rollback mechanisms must be in place
               * Monitoring and alerting are critical
               * Defective code can reach production if tests are insufficient
________________


Common Techniques Used
               * Canary Deployment – release to a small percentage of users first.
               * Blue-Green Deployment – switch traffic between two environments.
               * Rolling Updates – gradually replace old application instances.
               * Automatic Rollback – revert if health checks fail.
________________


Tools Commonly Used
               * Argo CD
               * Jenkins
               * GitHub Actions
               * GitLab CI/CD
               * Spinnaker
________________


Real-World Example (Kubernetes)
Developer Pushes Code
        ↓
GitHub Actions
        ↓
Build Docker Image
        ↓
Push to Registry
        ↓
ArgoCD Detects Change
        ↓
Deploy to GKE/EKS
        ↓
Health Checks Pass
        ↓
Release Live
________________


Interview Answer (1 Minute)
Continuous Deployment is a DevOps practice where every code change that successfully passes build, testing, quality, and security checks is automatically deployed to production without manual approval. It enables rapid and frequent software releases while reducing human intervention. To implement Continuous Deployment effectively, organizations need comprehensive automated testing, monitoring, and rollback mechanisms. In Kubernetes environments, tools such as Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Docker, and ArgoCD are commonly used to automate the entire deployment lifecycle.

questions.question: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
questions.answer: Continuous Delivery means every change that passes the pipeline is automatically packaged and ready to release, but a human still triggers the actual production release; Continuous Deployment goes one step further and releases every passing change to production automatically with no manual gate.

questions.question: Blue-green deployment: Explain blue-green deployment.
questions.answer:
Blue-green deployment is a release strategy where two identical production environments are maintained:


* Blue environment → current live production version
* Green environment → new version to be deployed


The new application or ML model version is deployed to the green environment while the blue environment continues serving live traffic.


Once testing and validation are successful, traffic is switched from blue to green with minimal downtime.


If any issue occurs after deployment, traffic can quickly be redirected back to the blue environment, making rollback fast and safe.


In MLOps and DevOps, blue-green deployment is commonly used to:


* Minimize downtime during releases
* Reduce deployment risk
* Enable fast rollback
* Validate new models or application versions safely


It is usually implemented using:


* Kubernetes services and ingress
* Load balancers
* CI/CD pipelines
* Cloud traffic management tools


Compared to canary deployment, blue-green deployment switches traffic completely between environments, while canary deployment gradually shifts traffic in phases.

questions.question: Canary deployment: Explain canary deployment.
questions.answer: Canary deployment routes a small percentage of production traffic to a new version while the majority continues to the stable version, allowing you to observe the new version's real-world behavior (error rate, latency, business metrics) on limited exposure before gradually increasing its traffic share or rolling back quickly if problems appear - it limits blast radius compared to deploying to 100% of traffic immediately.

questions.question: Have you worked on GCP, AWS, and Azure?
questions.answer: Answer with honest per-cloud depth rather than a blanket yes - e.g. 'primarily GCP day-to-day, working AWS knowledge from a past project, limited hands-on Azure' - since a vague 'yes to all three' invites deep follow-ups on whichever cloud you're weakest in.

questions.question: What is an Azure subscription?
questions.answer: An Azure subscription is a management and billing boundary for resources, with subscription-scoped quotas, policies and access assignments. It is associated with a Microsoft Entra tenant for identity and can contain resource groups that organize related resources. Organizations often separate subscriptions by environment, business unit or governance boundary and apply management-group policy across subscriptions. A subscription is not a subnet or an individual application runtime. Access still depends on the identity’s effective role at the relevant scope and applicable policies.

questions.question: What is the GCP equivalent of an Azure subscription?
questions.answer: A Google Cloud project is the closest practical equivalent for grouping resources and applying IAM, quotas and billing attribution. An Azure subscription is associated with an Entra tenant and a billing arrangement; a GCP project belongs in an organization/folder hierarchy and links to a billing account. The boundaries are similar rather than identical: compare specific IAM, billing and quota behavior when translating an architecture. Use management groups in Azure and folders/organization policies in GCP for governance across these resource containers.

questions.question: What is an Azure Network Security Group, and where can it be associated?
questions.answer: An NSG is a stateful Layer 3/4 traffic-filtering resource with prioritized inbound and outbound allow/deny rules based on protocol, source/destination and ports. It can be associated with a subnet and/or a supported network interface. If both apply, traffic must be permitted by the effective rules at both scopes. Smaller priority numbers are evaluated first, and default rules apply after custom rules. NSGs are not HTTP-aware WAFs and do not perform application authentication. Review effective security rules, routing and flow visibility when troubleshooting; allowing a port at the NSG alone does not prove the application is listening.

questions.question: What is Azure Application Gateway and how does its load-balancing role compare with GCP?
questions.answer: Azure Application Gateway is a regional HTTP/HTTPS application load balancer that supports host/path routing, TLS termination and an optional WAF tier. Azure Front Door is a different service for global edge routing. In Google Cloud, choose an Application Load Balancer with the appropriate global or regional and external or internal scope, configure URL maps and healthy backends, and use Cloud Armor where supported for WAF and edge policy. Products are not one-to-one replacements: verify scope, protocol support, private access and security integration before mapping an Azure design to GCP.

questions.question: Explain the Google Cloud Application Load Balancer.
questions.answer: An Application Load Balancer handles HTTP/HTTPS traffic at Layer 7. A forwarding rule/listener receives traffic, a target proxy handles protocol/TLS and a URL map selects a backend service by host/path and supported routing rules. Backend services reference supported backends such as instance groups, NEGs or serverless resources according to the load-balancer mode, and traffic goes to eligible healthy capacity. Select external/internal and global/regional scope deliberately; features are not identical across modes. Configure certificates, firewall/health-check requirements, logging, timeout settings and supported Cloud Armor policy. With GKE container-native NEGs, the data plane can route to Pod endpoints rather than traversing a ClusterIP.

questions.question: What security controls do you apply at an internet-facing Gateway or load balancer?
questions.answer: I use managed TLS, strong application authentication and authorization, Cloud Armor WAF and DDoS controls, per-route rate limits, request-size and timeout limits, and only required hosts, paths and methods. Backends remain private, headers are normalized carefully, and secrets are never trusted from the client. Access logs, audit logs, threat alerts and certificate monitoring feed incident response; policy changes begin in preview where possible.

questions.question: What is the difference between an Azure VM and VM Scale Sets, and what are their GCP equivalents?
questions.answer: An Azure VM is an individual virtual machine. VM Scale Sets manage a group of VM instances with orchestration, scaling and availability behavior according to the selected mode. The rough GCP equivalents are a Compute Engine VM and a Managed Instance Group using an instance template. A MIG can support autoscaling, health-check-driven autohealing and controlled rolling updates; regional MIGs can distribute instances across zones. Scaling a group does not automatically make a stateful application highly available: externalize durable state or design replication and lifecycle handling deliberately.

questions.question: Which databases have you worked on?
questions.answer: List with the actual operational depth for each - e.g. PostgreSQL (schema design, query tuning, backup/restore), managed Cloud SQL (mostly configuration, not deep engine internals), Redis (caching layer, not primary datastore) - since 'worked on' can mean anything from deep hands-on administration to just writing application queries against it, and the interviewer needs that distinction to ask the right follow-ups.

questions.question: What is the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?
questions.answer: IaaS supplies infrastructure such as VMs, networks and disks; the customer manages the guest operating system, application and much of its runtime. PaaS provides a managed application platform or runtime so the provider operates more of the OS and execution environment while the customer owns code, configuration and data. SaaS provides a finished application consumed by users, such as hosted email or CRM. Compute Engine/EC2, a managed application runtime such as Cloud Run, and a hosted productivity suite illustrate the progression. Responsibility shifts rather than disappears: identity, data classification, access configuration and appropriate use remain customer responsibilities in all three.

questions.question: What is TLS?
questions.answer:
TLS is a cryptographic protocol that secures network communication using encryption, certificate validation, and integrity checks. It replaced older SSL versions and is used by HTTPS, mTLS, and many service-to-service connections.

Detailed interview explanation:
TLS should be explained from a production troubleshooting and security perspective. These questions test whether you understand operating-system fundamentals, networking behavior, access control, and how to debug safely under pressure.

Production example:
If a service is slow or down, you may check service state with systemctl, logs with journalctl, processes with top or htop, memory with free and vmstat, disk with df and iostat, sockets with ss, DNS with dig, connectivity with curl or nc, and packets with tcpdump. For security topics, connect the answer to least privilege, hardening, encryption, segmentation, patching, and audit logs.

Best practices to mention:
- Start with impact, recent changes, logs, metrics, and resource saturation.
- Validate DNS, routes, firewall rules, TLS certificates, and dependency health for network issues.
- Use least privilege, patching, MFA, secrets management, and logging for security.
- Automate repetitive operational tasks with scripts and runbooks.
- Avoid risky production commands unless you understand blast radius and rollback.

Common interview follow-ups:
Interviewers may ask how to debug high CPU, memory leaks, disk full, inode exhaustion, DNS failures, packet loss, TLS issues, SSH access problems, or suspicious activity. Strong answers are step-by-step and evidence-driven.

questions.question: What is mTLS?
questions.answer:
mTLS, or mutual TLS, requires both client and server to present certificates. It provides encrypted communication plus strong service or user identity validation.

Detailed interview explanation:
Mtls should be explained from a production troubleshooting and security perspective. These questions test whether you understand operating-system fundamentals, networking behavior, access control, and how to debug safely under pressure.

Production example:
If a service is slow or down, you may check service state with systemctl, logs with journalctl, processes with top or htop, memory with free and vmstat, disk with df and iostat, sockets with ss, DNS with dig, connectivity with curl or nc, and packets with tcpdump. For security topics, connect the answer to least privilege, hardening, encryption, segmentation, patching, and audit logs.

Best practices to mention:
- Start with impact, recent changes, logs, metrics, and resource saturation.
- Validate DNS, routes, firewall rules, TLS certificates, and dependency health for network issues.
- Use least privilege, patching, MFA, secrets management, and logging for security.
- Automate repetitive operational tasks with scripts and runbooks.
- Avoid risky production commands unless you understand blast radius and rollback.

Common interview follow-ups:
Interviewers may ask how to debug high CPU, memory leaks, disk full, inode exhaustion, DNS failures, packet loss, TLS issues, SSH access problems, or suspicious activity. Strong answers are step-by-step and evidence-driven.

questions.question: What is the difference between TLS and mTLS?
questions.answer: TLS protects a connection with encryption and integrity and normally authenticates the server using a certificate validated by the client. Mutual TLS additionally requires the client to present a certificate that the server validates, providing authentication in both directions. A service mesh can automate workload certificate issuance, rotation and mTLS between services. mTLS proves an authenticated peer identity; application authorization still decides which operations it may perform. Validate trust chains, certificate expiry and identities, and account for TLS termination boundaries when explaining an end-to-end request path.

questions.question: Can you start with your introduction?
questions.answer: I am a DevOps/SRE engineer focused on reliable cloud platforms, infrastructure automation and production operations. My core experience spans GCP, Terraform, GKE, CI/CD, observability, incident response and Python or Bash automation. I briefly connect my current responsibilities, one measurable reliability or delivery outcome, and why this role is the logical next step, keeping the introduction relevant rather than reciting my resume.

questions.question: Which project are you currently working on?
questions.answer: Name the project, its business purpose in one sentence, your specific role on it (not the whole team's role), and the technologies involved. If it's still in progress, mention the current phase and the next milestone - interviewers use this to gauge whether you can clearly scope and communicate ongoing work.

questions.question: A GKE deployment succeeded and application logs are visible, but users receive 502 or 503 errors. How would you troubleshoot pods, probes, Services, endpoints, Ingress, NEGs, backends, firewalls and NetworkPolicies?
questions.answer: I trace one request from DNS and frontend to the Pod and identify which component emitted the status. I verify the expected Deployment revision, available replicas, readiness and recent events; a running Pod is not necessarily ready. I test the application on its container port and check whether the readiness path, protocol and timing reflect real serving health. I inspect the Service selector, port and targetPort, then EndpointSlices to confirm ready Pod IPs exist. From an approved debug Pod I test Service DNS and direct endpoint connectivity. At the GKE edge I inspect Ingress or Gateway events, URL map, backend service, NEG membership and backend health, including health-check port and path. A 503 often means no healthy backend or exhausted capacity; a 502 often indicates a bad upstream response, reset, protocol or timeout, but I confirm from logs rather than assuming. I verify health-check and data-plane firewall access plus NetworkPolicy ingress from the actual source. After correcting the smallest fault, I validate external traffic, latency and errors and add a deployment or monitoring gate for the missed condition.

questions.question: How would you enforce and monitor Kubernetes egress after a security incident?
questions.answer: Inventory required destinations and inspect current DNS, flow and proxy logs before tightening rules. Apply default-deny egress with a NetworkPolicy-capable dataplane, then allow the exact DNS and service/database destinations needed by each workload. Standard NetworkPolicy primarily selects Pods, namespaces and IP blocks; it does not provide portable domain-name or HTTP URL filtering. For public domains or Layer-7 controls use a supported egress gateway, firewall or proxy and force traffic through it with routing/policy; prevent bypass through node networking, hostNetwork workloads or uncontrolled privileged Pods. Cloud NAT supplies outbound address translation and is not an authorization policy by itself. Combine cloud firewall controls, workload identity, TLS validation, approved proxies, deny logs and alerts on new destinations or unusual transfer volumes. Roll out in observation/test stages where supported, test allowed and blocked paths, and document time-bound exceptions.

questions.question: How would you detect a regional API failure and fail over DNS-routed traffic?
questions.answer: Use independent synthetic probes and regional application/business SLIs, not only VM health, with quorum and failure thresholds to avoid flapping. Confirm the surviving region has capacity and a writable, sufficiently current data tier; fence the old writer if necessary to prevent split brain. Route health checks disable unhealthy regional records according to the DNS provider’s failover policy. DNS caching and existing connections mean failover is not instantaneous even with a low TTL, so measure observed client recovery rather than promising the TTL as the RTO. Prepare runbooks for automated versus operator-authorized failover, replication-lag limits, transaction safety and customer updates. Test regional isolation and gradual failback after data reconciliation. Where requirements demand faster routing decisions, evaluate a global application load balancer rather than relying solely on DNS.

questions.question: What risks would you assess in a multi-region application provisioned with Infrastructure as Code?
questions.answer: IaC makes resources reproducible but does not by itself make an application resilient. Check whether regions share a single database writer, secrets/key service, CI runner, state backend or network dependency; one common failure can defeat regional redundancy. Review state isolation, provider/resource region selection, quotas and reserved capacity, configuration drift, version compatibility, replicated data and measurable RPO/RTO. Ensure traffic failover respects data readiness and that writes cannot split brain. Pre-provision critical standby components because APIs, quota or capacity may be unavailable during a disaster. Test region-loss drills, restore procedures and failback; use Terraform for declarative recovery while separate automation handles data promotion and routing decisions.

questions.question: How would you replace in-place VM application updates that cause drift and difficult rollbacks?
questions.answer: Build a versioned, tested machine image or immutable application artifact, then create a new instance template/launch template and a separate replacement pool. Boot the new instances with externally managed environment configuration and secrets, verify readiness and warm caches, and gradually shift load-balancer traffic. Use rolling replacement or blue-green according to spare capacity and rollback requirements. Drain existing connections before removing old instances. Roll back by restoring traffic to the retained healthy pool or deploying its pinned template version. Persist business data outside disposable VM disks and keep database/API changes backward compatible. Record image, configuration and template versions together so rebuilding a pool reproduces the tested release.

questions.question: How would you safely introduce a microservice beside a billing system where errors could duplicate charges or lose transactions?
questions.answer: First protect correctness with idempotency keys, unique transaction constraints, auditable ledger entries, reconciliation and explicit retry semantics. A canary limits exposure but cannot undo a customer charge, so validate contracts and migrations, use test accounts and shadow traffic only when it cannot create side effects, and put billing actions behind a kill switch. Start with a tightly controlled cohort and monitor payment correctness, duplicate rate and reconciliation, not just HTTP success. Expand only after business validation; stop traffic and disable the feature on a financial mismatch. Keep old/new service and schema versions compatible and prepare compensating actions for committed transactions because a software rollback does not roll back external payments.

questions.question: How do you investigate latency across Kubernetes microservices using Istio and distributed tracing?
questions.answer: Start from the affected endpoint, time range and p95/p99 latency, then compare successful and slow traces using propagated trace IDs. Locate the first long span and separate application execution, downstream waiting, database queries, queueing and network/connect time. Compare Envoy upstream request time, response flags, retries, pending requests, connection-pool limits and outlier ejections with application and node metrics. Check VirtualService/DestinationRule changes, routing subsets, mTLS failures, DNS and cross-zone/region calls; mesh retries can amplify load and hide the first error. Validate whether tracing is sampled or missing spans before concluding a dependency is fast. Mitigate the evidenced bottleneck with a narrow rollback, bounded retries or concurrency control, then confirm business success and latency recover without shifting overload downstream.

questions.question: What would you do in the first five minutes when a load-balancer target group is failing?
questions.answer: Declare/acknowledge the incident, capture customer impact and identify the affected listener/rule, target group and unhealthy reason codes. Check recent deployments, target registration, port and protocol, health-check path, TLS, security rules and the number of healthy targets. Stop an ongoing rollout and retain evidence. If known-good healthy capacity exists, shift traffic or restore the previous backend configuration under the incident procedure; drain a demonstrably faulty subset rather than removing all backends. Confirm the destination region has capacity and the correct data role before regional failover. Avoid weakening health checks merely to make targets appear healthy. Validate real requests, error rate, latency and healthy-target count, record the change and communicate the next checkpoint.

questions.question: How do you design microservice or model health checks and isolate failure domains?
questions.answer: Separate startup checks from liveness and readiness. Startup allows initialization or model loading; liveness detects an unrecoverable local process problem; readiness indicates whether the instance can accept traffic. Do not make liveness depend on a shared database or model API because a downstream outage could restart the entire fleet. Readiness should exercise necessary local capability without expensive work on every probe, while independent synthetics test end-to-end business correctness and model quality. Spread replicas across nodes/zones, set deadlines and retry budgets, and isolate pools/queues so one tenant or dependency cannot exhaust all capacity. Test node, zone and dependency failures and measure which user journeys remain available.

questions.question: How would you substantiate a claim that Terraform standardization reduced provisioning effort by 70%, and why might automation not reach 100%?
questions.answer: Define the measured unit first: engineer-hours per comparable environment, request lead time or number of manual steps. For example, reducing hands-on work from 10 hours to 3 hours is a 70% reduction, calculated as (baseline minus new effort) divided by baseline times 100; that does not prove a 70% reduction in calendar lead time. Compare similar requests over a stated period and include failed/reworked runs and ongoing platform maintenance. Versioned modules, policy checks and repeatable pipelines can remove repetitive provisioning. Architecture decisions, unusual exceptions, access approval, production risk acceptance and business validation may still require people. Attribute only the work you personally performed and use records rather than invented percentages.

questions.question: How would you replicate an AWS-hosted database in Mumbai to GCP, and where does Datastream CDC fit?
questions.answer:
Confirm engine/version, data volume, schema features, target service, acceptable downtime, RPO and cross-cloud transfer cost before choosing a tool. Establish encrypted private or tightly restricted connectivity, configure a least-privilege replication identity and the source log settings, and test bandwidth and latency. CDC reads changes from database logs after a consistent initial backfill, retaining a checkpoint so interrupted replication resumes. Google Datastream is a managed CDC service; choose only supported source/destination combinations and do not assume it directly replicates any database into Cloud SQL or AlloyDB. For a transactional database migration, evaluate Database Migration Service or supported native/logical replication for that engine and target. Monitor replication lag and log retention, compare row counts/checksums and application behavior, then stop writes or coordinate a controlled cutover, catch up, switch endpoints and validate. Document rollback and how post-cutover writes would be reconciled.

References: https://docs.cloud.google.com/datastream/docs/destinations

questions.question: Which AWS services have you worked with so far?
questions.answer: My AWS experience includes EC2 for compute, S3 for object storage, IAM for access control, VPC networking and security groups, CloudFormation stacks for infrastructure as code, CloudFront for content delivery, Lambda for event-driven functions, EventBridge for schedules and event routing, CloudWatch for logs and metrics, and related load-balancing and container services where required. I connect each service to an actual workflow rather than reciting a list—for example, an EventBridge rule invoking Lambda to process an S3 event, with IAM least privilege, CloudWatch alarms, retries and a dead-letter path. GCP is my deeper current platform, so I state AWS depth honestly and explain how the architecture and operating principles transfer across clouds.

questions.question: What is Route 53?
questions.answer: Amazon Route 53 is AWS’s scalable, highly available Domain Name System (DNS) and domain-registration service. It manages public and private hosted zones, standard DNS record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV), and Alias records that map names directly to AWS resources (ELB, CloudFront, S3). Route 53 provides routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, multi-value answer) plus health checks and DNS-based failover. It also offers Route 53 Resolver for VPC DNS resolution and inbound/outbound endpoints to connect on‑prem networks. Operate via Console, Route 53 APIs, or AWS CLI (e.g., aws route53 create-hosted-zone; aws route53 change-resource-record-sets; aws route53 list-health-checks) to verify configuration and health.

questions.question: How do Route 53 private hosted zones and hybrid DNS resolution work?
questions.answer: A private hosted zone provides records to VPCs associated with the zone through the VPC Route 53 Resolver; the records are not published into public DNS. Enable the required VPC DNS settings and confirm zone association and the most-specific matching namespace. For on-premises clients resolving AWS private names, use inbound Resolver endpoints reachable over VPN/Direct Connect and conditional forwarding from the on-premises DNS servers. For VPC clients resolving on-premises names, associate forwarding rules with the VPC and send queries through outbound Resolver endpoints to on-premises DNS. Allow both UDP and TCP 53, use redundant endpoint addresses and avoid forwarding loops. DNS resolution does not itself provide network routing or permission to connect to the resolved service.

questions.question: What can NGINX or Apache do for rate limiting and suspicious paths, and why are they insufficient for large DDoS attacks?
questions.answer: An NGINX reverse proxy can apply request-rate and connection limits, allowlists and explicit deny rules for unwanted paths, such as a PHP administration URL on a service that has no PHP application. Apache needs appropriate modules or a WAF/proxy integration for the desired request-rate policy; mod_ratelimit alone limits response bandwidth rather than requests per second. Authenticate callers and choose a suitable limit key, trusting forwarded client IP headers only from known proxies. Tune limits to avoid blocking shared-NAT users or legitimate bursts, and log decisions. These controls operate after traffic reaches the server or network and cannot recover bandwidth already saturated by a volumetric attack. Upstream provider filtering, CDN/edge controls or DDoS scrubbing are required for that threat. A few path rules are not equivalent to full WAF coverage.

questions.question: An EKS application suddenly reports a configuration error without a deployment. What would you investigate?
questions.answer: Preserve the error and time range, identify affected Pods/nodes and compare healthy replicas. Run kubectl get pods -o wide, kubectl describe pod, kubectl logs --previous where relevant, kubectl get events and inspect Deployment revisions, ConfigMap/Secret metadata and Service/EndpointSlice selectors. No application release does not mean no change: secret rotation, configuration reloads, certificate expiry, IAM changes, node replacement, DNS updates and external database changes can all break the service. Check CloudTrail/Kubernetes audit trails for writers and controller actions without printing secret values. Compare mounted files versus environment variables, service-account identity, DNS and connectivity from a permitted debug context. Fix or revert the identified configuration or dependency through the incident process and confirm both new and surviving Pods recover.

questions.question: Design a three-tier application on AWS.
questions.answer: Web tier: an Application Load Balancer in public subnets fronting an Auto Scaling Group of web servers. Application tier: a second internal ALB or service discovery routing to an Auto Scaling Group of app servers in private subnets, with no direct internet access. Data tier: RDS (Multi-AZ for HA) in private subnets with security groups only allowing traffic from the app tier. Each tier sits in its own subnet with security groups scoped to only the traffic that tier actually needs from the tier above it.

questions.question: How would you add CI/CD, monitoring, backup and DR to a three-tier application?
questions.answer: Build and test the web/application artifacts once, scan/sign them and promote the same version through staged environments with approval and rollback. Provision networks, compute, database and identities through reviewed IaC and keep runtime secrets outside source code. Monitor customer availability/latency, dependency failures, saturation and database health with correlated logs and traces. Use multi-zone application capacity and a supported highly available database configuration, but also protect data with retained backups/PITR and restore tests. Define RTO/RPO for regional loss and rehearse recovery into independent capacity with replicated images, configuration and keys. Record ownership and runbooks so delivery and recovery are executable, not merely boxes on an architecture diagram.

questions.question: Does a database in a GCP subnet without Cloud NAT need NAT to communicate privately with an application subnet?
questions.answer: No. Within the same VPC, subnet routes provide private connectivity subject to firewall rules and application listening configuration, even when the subnets are in different regions. Cloud NAT is generally used for outbound access to external destinations from resources without external IPs; it is not required for ordinary private traffic between subnets. If the database is a managed Cloud SQL or AlloyDB service, verify its supported private connectivity mechanism, such as Private Services Access or Private Service Connect, rather than assuming it is an ordinary VM in a customer subnet. Across different VPCs or projects, configure an actual shared or connected network path and DNS. Private routing, DNS, firewall policy and database authentication all need to work independently.

questions.question: What happens when teams mix google_project_iam_policy, google_project_iam_binding and google_project_iam_member, and how do you prevent IAM conflicts?
questions.answer: google_project_iam_policy authoritatively manages the project allow policy and can remove grants managed elsewhere. google_project_iam_binding authoritatively manages members for a particular role binding, including the relevant condition, while google_project_iam_member adds an individual member grant without owning the whole role membership. A full-policy resource must not compete with binding/member resources for the same project; a binding must not compete with separate member resources for that same binding. Competing owners cause recurring diffs, overwritten access and possible lockout. Establish one state/owner for each authoritative scope, use additive member grants for delegated application access where appropriate, review plans and test access before changes. Import existing intended grants when adopting ownership and avoid broad policy replacement merely to add one identity.

questions.question: How would you design centralized networking in GCP when you have multiple projects, such as SAP Dev, UAT, and Production projects?
questions.answer: I would use a dedicated Shared VPC host project owned by the networking team and attach SAP Dev, UAT, and Production as service projects. Central subnets, routes, Cloud NAT, DNS, hybrid connectivity, firewall policies, flow logs, and load-balancing controls stay in the host project, while application resources and lifecycle remain in the service projects. I would normally isolate production from non-production with separate Shared VPC host projects or at least strongly separated subnets, firewall policies, IAM, and routing domains when the risk model permits one host. Access is delegated with least-privilege Shared VPC roles, and Terraform plus policy checks manages attachments and network changes. Centralized inspection, logging, IP planning, and controlled connectivity to on-premises SAP dependencies complete the design.

questions.question: Can you explain the enterprise-scale GCP architecture you designed, including the organization, projects, networking, security and shared services?
questions.answer: I structured the platform from the organization root into folders aligned to governance boundaries such as platform, production, non-production and sandbox, with business-unit folders where delegation required them. Separate projects created IAM, quota, billing and blast-radius boundaries for applications, Shared VPC hosts, security, centralized logging, CI/CD and common services. A project factory used versioned Terraform modules to create projects, enable APIs, attach billing, apply labels and budgets, configure logging sinks and inherit Organization Policies. Central host projects provided Shared VPC subnets, IP planning, DNS, Cloud NAT, hybrid connectivity and hierarchical firewall controls, with production separated from lower environments. Identity was federated and group-based; workloads used Workload Identity instead of keys; privileged access was time-bound; secrets and encryption keys had dedicated ownership. Security Command Center, audit logs, asset inventory and monitoring flowed into protected central projects and the SIEM. GKE golden paths included private clusters, policy enforcement, signed images, network policies, autoscaling, backups and GitOps. Exceptions were reviewed, expiring and visible. I measured onboarding time, policy compliance, reliability and cost, treating the landing zone as an operated platform product.

questions.question: How would you design regional disaster recovery with an RTO of 30 minutes and RPO of 5 minutes?
questions.answer: Use another region because another zone in the same region does not cover region-wide failure. Keep a warm standby with critical networks, IAM, keys, images, application capacity and data replication already configured; on-demand creation alone may miss the RTO due to quotas, capacity or API outages. RPO 5 minutes requires monitored cross-region replication or backup/log-shipping intervals and restore capability that actually meet that bound; asynchronous replication can exceed it, so alert on lag and define how to handle the breach. RTO includes detection, authorization, fencing the old writer, promoting data, scaling the standby, changing traffic and validating transactions. Terraform reproduces/configures infrastructure but does not automatically promote a database or guarantee recovery time. Run timed drills, validate backups and application dependencies, and plan reconciliation and failback. Separate actual implementation experience from a proposed design.

questions.question: What would you discuss about Veeam and Kasten K10 disaster recovery without overstating hands-on experience?
questions.answer: State whether you operated the product, assisted a backup team or only know the design. Veeam is commonly used for protected workload backup and recovery, while Kasten K10 addresses Kubernetes application backup, restore and mobility. For Kubernetes, inventory manifests, persistent volumes, application-consistent hooks, secrets and external database dependencies; a volume snapshot alone may be crash-consistent or remain in the failed region. Verify independent backup storage, encryption/key access, retention, permissions and restore into a separate cluster/region. Measure restore duration and data loss using a real application validation, not only a completed backup job. A personal example needs the actual workload, ownership, test outcome and lessons learned.

questions.question: How do you fix an incorrect ECS environment variable during a production outage without rebuilding the image or bypassing accountability?
questions.answer: Confirm the failing variable and a known-good value without exposing secrets. Declare the incident and obtain the documented emergency-change authority, recording the approver, exact change and rollback. Register a new task-definition revision using the same immutable image digest but corrected environment configuration or secret reference, then update the ECS service to that revision. A value in a running task is not changed simply by editing the source secret; launch replacement tasks according to the integration behavior. Monitor health and business requests during rollout and revert the service to the last known-good task-definition revision if needed. Use scoped, time-bound break-glass access only when the procedure requires it. Immediately reconcile the emergency change into Git/IaC with a reviewed follow-up so the next normal deployment does not restore the error.

questions.question: How do you retain container images and make production rollback reliable?
questions.answer: Retain every image digest currently deployed and the validated rollback digests, along with deployment manifests, configuration/schema compatibility and build provenance. The retention count follows the release rate, rollback window, regulatory needs and storage budget; keeping the last 5–10 releases can be an example policy but is not universally sufficient. Tags are convenient labels and may move, so deploy and record immutable digests; latest is not a reproducible release identifier. Exempt active/rollback artifacts from cleanup and test restoration in a lower environment. Retain compatible configuration and database migration paths because an old image alone may not safely run against the current schema. For a vulnerable rollback version, assess risk and prepare a corrected known-good release rather than assuming retention implies approval.

questions.question: How do Prometheus, Loki, Logstash, Grafana and Alertmanager fit together in observability?
questions.answer: Prometheus collects numerical time-series metrics, typically by scraping instrumented endpoints, and evaluates recording/alerting rules. Loki stores and queries logs with labels and log content; logs provide individual event detail while metrics summarize rates, latency and saturation. Logstash is a processing pipeline that receives, parses, enriches and forwards events to destinations such as Elasticsearch; it is not the same kind of metrics store as Prometheus. Grafana visualizes and correlates data from these systems and can run its own alerting. Alertmanager receives alerts, groups/deduplicates them and handles routing, inhibition and silences. Define shared service/environment labels and correlation IDs, control cardinality and sensitive data, and page on actionable user impact.

questions.question: How do you justify a claimed 20% cloud cost reduction?
questions.answer: Choose a comparable baseline and period and separate usage changes, price/discount changes and architectural savings. If normalized monthly cost falls from 100,000 to 80,000 in the same currency, the reduction is 20%; use actual billing exports and allocation labels rather than this illustrative number in a personal answer. Investigate idle resources, oversized requests/VMs, unused disks/IPs, log retention, cross-region egress, non-production schedules and stable demand eligible for commitments. Explain which changes contributed and avoid double-counting overlapping savings. Compare cost per transaction or other business unit alongside total spend and verify SLOs, latency and capacity remained acceptable. State whether the 20% is realized recurring savings or a forecast and whether it includes implementation costs.

questions.question: How would you migrate a monolithic GitHub repository to Bitbucket while preserving history and validating cutover?
questions.answer: Inventory repositories, refs, LFS objects, submodules, release assets, CI configuration, webhooks, credentials and access controls. Keep repository migration separate from splitting a monolith unless there is an explicit tested restructuring plan. In a controlled temporary clone, git clone --mirror and git push --mirror can transfer Git refs; use them only against the intended empty destination because mirror push can delete destination refs. Transfer LFS objects separately with git lfs fetch --all and git lfs push --all using secured authentication. Git history does not include hosted PR discussions, issues, permissions or CI secrets, so migrate or archive those explicitly. Compare branch/tag object IDs, verify Git object integrity and perform clean checkouts including LFS/submodules; run CI and test protections/webhooks. Freeze source writes, do a final sync, cut over remotes/integrations and keep the source read-only with a documented rollback window.

questions.question: How would you plan and validate an EKS upgrade from Kubernetes 1.32 to 1.36?
questions.answer:
Treat 1.36 as a target to verify against EKS availability and support in the intended region. Upgrade one minor version at a time: 1.32 to 1.33 to 1.34 to 1.35 to 1.36. Before each step inspect upgrade insights/deprecated APIs, webhook compatibility, node/runtime versions and supported VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, CSI and controller versions. Back up declarative resources and application data and rehearse restore; managed control-plane backups are not a customer-operated etcd rollback plan. Follow the documented control-plane/add-on/node sequencing, ensure spare capacity and drain nodes within PDB and storage constraints. After each version verify API health, DNS, ingress, networking, volumes, autoscaling and business transactions, then pause on regression. Check the currently supported rollback options and restrictions rather than assuming downgrades are always available. A blue-green cluster migration can provide a clearer traffic rollback path but requires tested data and workload migration.

References: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/update-cluster.html

questions.question: Why might the latest EKS node AMI fail in production after a POC passed, and how would you investigate and roll back?
questions.answer: An AMI label such as latest is a moving target. Compare exact AMI IDs, OS/kernel, containerd, cgroups, kubelet, bootstrap parameters, CNI/CSI, security agents, instance family, architecture and user data between environments. Capture node events, journalctl -k, dmesg, kubelet/runtime logs and cloud serial console output where permitted; distinguish kernel panic, OOM, driver failure and networking regression. Stop further rollout and create a replacement node group pinned to the previously validated image/template if it remains compatible with the control plane. Cordon and drain faulty nodes with capacity and PDB checks, then validate storage/networking and representative traffic. Promote the same tested AMI through environments, canary new node images and retain provenance instead of silently resolving latest during production creation.

questions.question: How do frontend and backend containers on separate VMs communicate, and how is VM networking different from Docker networking?
questions.answer: First ensure VM private addressing, routes and firewall/security-group rules allow the intended backend port only from approved sources. On the backend host publish the container port on an appropriate host interface, for example host-private-IP:8080 to container port 8080, and ensure the process listens on the container interface. A bridge network is normally local to one Docker host; two hosts using the same bridge name are not connected by that name. The frontend server calls a private DNS name resolving to the backend host or internal load balancer, using the published service port and TLS/authentication as required. A browser-based frontend executes on the user device, so it cannot normally reach private VM IPs; expose a public API through a controlled gateway or a same-origin reverse proxy. Debug host reachability and container publishing separately.

questions.question: How do you provide a stable backend endpoint when VM IP addresses change?
questions.answer: Expose the backend through an internal load balancer and a private DNS service name, then register healthy replacement instances in its backend group. Clients depend on a service endpoint rather than a disposable VM address. A reserved static private IP can help for a single host but does not provide failover or eliminate dependency on that host. Restrict permissions that delete forwarding rules, reservations or records, manage them in IaC and monitor endpoint health. Use connection draining and compatible old/new instances during replacement; account for DNS TTLs and pooled connections. For browser clients, the public gateway should call the private backend so private addresses are not exposed as client-reachable URLs.

questions.question: Explain the complete request path for an e-commerce Place Order operation.
questions.answer: The browser calls a public HTTPS API such as https://shop.example.com/api/orders, normally through a same-origin frontend or approved API hostname. DNS resolves the gateway/load-balancer address, not a Docker network name or an individual database. TLS, edge WAF/rate controls and request routing lead to an authenticated and authorized backend. The backend validates the cart, prices and inventory server-side, uses an idempotency key to guard retries, writes the order transaction to its database and coordinates payment/inventory through a transaction or reliable outbox/workflow. Database connections use private connectivity and least-privilege credentials; the browser never receives database credentials. Return a defined status and order ID, and correlate gateway, service and database telemetry using trace IDs. Handle partial failures with explicit retry/compensation and reconciliation rather than assuming a distributed transaction is atomic.

questions.question: Docker experience: Have you worked on Docker? Explain the workflows and production concerns you handled.
questions.answer: Production Docker workflows typically involve writing multi-stage Dockerfiles for small, secure images, integrating vulnerability scanning and image signing into the CI pipeline, and pushing versioned images to a registry consumed by Kubernetes deployments. Production concerns include ensuring images run as non-root, resource limits are set correctly at the orchestration layer, base images are kept patched and current, and build reproducibility is maintained through pinned dependencies and digests rather than floating tags.

questions.question: Explain the request flow from the Internet through the load balancer or Gateway and Kubernetes to the application.
questions.answer: DNS resolves the hostname to the load-balancer frontend. TLS terminates at the proxy, security policy is evaluated and the URL map selects a backend from the matching Gateway and HTTPRoute host/path rules. The backend service chooses a healthy NEG endpoint, and traffic reaches the ready Pod IP and target port. The response returns through the proxy; logs and traces correlate every layer.

questions.question: How would you create 10 EC2 instances using Terraform?
In Terraform, how do you specify the number of EC2 instances and output the created count and instance IDs?
questions.answer: With count, declare a validated non-negative integer input and set count = var.server_count on aws_instance.server. The Terraform expressions length(aws_instance.server) and aws_instance.server[*].id produce the managed instance count and list of IDs. Example outputs are: output "created_count" { value = length(aws_instance.server) } and output "instance_ids" { value = aws_instance.server[*].id }. The IDs are unknown until creation if the instances do not yet exist. This counts resources in that Terraform configuration/state, not all live EC2 instances in the account. For independently named servers, for_each over a stable-key map avoids index shifts when removing an element; derive IDs with a for expression over the map. Confirm desired count in plan before apply.

questions.question: CrashLoopBackOff: A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff in production. Give me your exact Kubernetes troubleshooting workflow and the commands or signals you would check.
questions.answer: Start with `kubectl describe pod` to see recent events and the last termination reason/exit code, then `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` to see the crashed container's actual output before it died. Check the exit code specifically (137 usually means OOMKilled, 1 or other application-specific codes point to an app-level crash), verify resource limits aren't too low if OOMKilled, check readiness/liveness probe configuration if the crash is probe-induced, and confirm any mounted ConfigMap/Secret dependencies are correctly present.

questions.question: How would you explain your L1/L2 SRE level and daily responsibilities?
questions.answer: The meaning of L1 and L2 varies by organization. L1 commonly triages alerts and follows established runbooks; L2 usually investigates deeper production issues, coordinates specialists, restores services and improves automation/runbooks. My personal response would identify my actual rota, systems, access level and escalation boundaries, then describe one task or incident I owned. Typical SRE work includes SLO review, incident follow-up, capacity planning, deployment safety and reducing operational toil. Team labels and years of experience are not substitutes for concrete responsibility, and I would not claim incident-command or production-admin ownership if it belonged to another team.
